name: Borth coastal defence reef (multi-purpose reef, Phase 1), Ceredigion, Wales

confidence.reason: The two mounds are clearly visible as bare rock on four dated, geo-referenced Esri images (2012-2024) and the outline agrees in position (0.3-4 m), orientation (1-3 deg) and length (-4 % north, +0.4 % south) with the georeferenced Royal Haskoning construction plan and with a 2022 Welsh Government LiDAR survey. The area is the visible rock edge only: 18 % smaller than the design armour-foot polygon and 34 % smaller than the LiDAR exposed footprint, so the true toe is larger than drawn.
factors: + four independent geo-referenced images, no change 2012-2024 (IoU 2024/2022 0.84; 2012 shifted 5 m by imagery registration)
+ design plan (15 setting-out points in OS grid, residual 0.02 m) overlays the satellite: IoU 0.79 N / 0.86 S, centroids within 4 m
+ LiDAR (as-built, 1 m) confirms crest levels and the two-mound layout
- no published text length/width exists (only 300/400 m offshore); the 'text' check is against the design drawing
- area depends on the waterline: drawn 5,743 m2 vs design foot 6,989 m2 vs LiDAR 8,675 m2
- absolute position uncertainty about +-5 m (Esri; OSGB36->WGS84 Helmert 2-5 m)

design_version.drawn: As-built FINAL layout of Phase 1 (completed March 2012): northern surf reef = boot/hook-shaped rock reef, southern oval = 'Southern Reef' / shore-parallel breakwater; outline = visible rock edge on 2012-2024 imagery (primary 2024-09-17)
design_version.why_this_one: It is the layout that was built: the Royal Haskoning 'For Construction' plan (rev C1, Jan 2011) matches the imagery (IoU 0.79 / 0.86) and the footprint is unchanged on imagery 2012-10, 2013-06, 2022-08, 2024-09 and in the 2022 LiDAR. Phase 1 was completed in 2012 (Coflein 8 March 2012; Ceredigion monitoring report 2013). No later extension, repair or damage was found (Phase 2, 2013-15, is rock breakwaters and groynes along the village frontage north of the reef; the 2020 Borth-Ynyslas outline business case concerns the frontage to the north).

alternatives_seen.what: Original design 2008-09: two surfable geotube reefs, northern 'truncated delta' 180 x 65 m, 4.0 m high, crest about MSL, plus a southern reef B (HRPP576 Figs 2-3)
alternatives_seen.why_not_used: superseded: physical modelling showed cross waves between the reefs; B was replaced by the shore-parallel breakwater C, the northern reef was extended and built in rock

alternatives_seen.what: Gemini's 'double reef' 200 x 65 m, 12,500 m2, units of 120 x 45 m and 180 x 65 m, 200 m offshore
alternatives_seen.why_not_used: no source; contradicted by the construction drawings and the imagery (see gemini block)
none found affecting the reef: Phase 2 (2013-15) is north of it; imagery and LiDAR show the same two mounds 2012-2024

gemini.summary: Gemini's two-unit 'double reef' topology is right, but nearly every number is wrong or unsourced. Offshore distance 200 m: built 330 m (sources say 300 / 400 m). 200 x 65 m / 12,500 m2: the built structure is a 145-150 m boot-shaped reef (outer toe 166 x 65 m) plus a 72 x 32 m oval (2033 m2 foot); visible rock 5,743 m2, armour foot 6,989 m2. Crest -1.5 m CD and seabed -6.8 m: the design crests are ABOVE ordnance datum (+0.50 / +1.00 / +1.50 mODN = +2.94 / +3.44 / +3.94 m above chart datum) on a seabed of about -4.0 mODN (-1.6 m CD); height about 4.5 m (north) and 5.1-5.7 m (south) above the seabed (Gemini 5.3 m). Designer 'Halcrow' is wrong: Royal Haskoning (with ASR; HR Wallingford modelling). Shoreline orientation 025 deg is wrong: the frontage runs N-S (359.6 deg). The south mound is a shore-parallel breakwater / 'Southern Reef' (crest +1.50 mODN), not an 'auxiliary mound' 120 x 45 m. Tidal range 4.8 m is the largest spring range; the mean spring range from the design levels is 4.30 m. Gemini's three cited documents could not be found; none of the sources it names gives a length, width or depth.

outline_versions.name: Laser survey edge (Welsh Government LiDAR, 19 Mar 2022)
outline_versions.method: 1 m LiDAR DSM (lightly smoothed, sigma 0.8 m) inside the exposed-rock outline; below the water edge the Royal Haskoning toe-berm slopes (1:1.5), 2 m flat blanket and 1:1.5 blanket edge (drawings 1021-1023) down to the modelled seabed.
outline_versions.level: rock exposed at the water level during the flight (about -2.3 mODN)
outline_versions.note: Default (Lior 2026-10-06: laser survey or rock layer are more accurate than a photo). DSM sees block tops, about 0.1-0.3 m above the design surface.

outline_versions.name: Design rock-layer foot (Royal Haskoning drawing 9V5090/1020 rev C1, Jan 2011)
outline_versions.method: Design surface lofted from the crest outline (setting-out points R1-R15, crest levels +0.50 / +1.00 / +0.00 ramp / +1.50) down to the armour foot ring at -2.15 mODN, then the toe berm (1.35 m, 1:1.5), 2 m blanket apron and blanket edge rings of drawing 1020, onto the modelled seabed.
outline_versions.level: foot of the Type 4 armour layer = top of the toe berm (about -2.15 mODN)
outline_versions.note: The as-designed rock layer; the as-built flanks are flatter and 8-10 m wider than the design (LiDAR).

outline_versions.name: Visible rock edge (Esri satellite photo, 17 Sep 2024)
outline_versions.method: Traced rock edge (79 vertices) as the footprint; LiDAR DSM inside; design toe slopes below the edge (assumed 1:1.5 from the edge down to the bed, i.e. steeper than the real flanks).
outline_versions.level: bare rock above the waterline in the photo (about -1.3 mODN from the DSM at the traced edge)
outline_versions.note: Smallest footprint: the photo shows only the rock above the water at that tide, so it understates the structure; kept as the traceable photo outline.

versions_info: Three outlines of the same two rock mounds. Default: the laser-survey edge (Welsh Government LiDAR, flown 19 March 2022 at about the lowest spring tide): the rock exposed at water level, 8,675 m2, built from the LiDAR surface plus the design toe slopes (a measured surface is more accurate than a photo). Second: the design rock-layer foot of Royal Haskoning drawing 9V5090/1020 (Jan 2011), 6,989 m2. Third: the visible rock edge in the Esri photo of 17 Sep 2024, 5,743 m2, the outline that was traced first and is kept for traceability. Areas differ because the three edges sit at different heights on the same sloping flanks, not because the structure moved.
outline_versions_chosen: Lior chose the LiDAR default on 2026-10-06 (laser survey or rock layer are more accurate than a photo); canonical.polygons_m stays the traced polygon.
